turn_text: The two things I hear the most often are the economy and the condition of the Sierra Nevada. My district pretty much is the Sierra Nevada of California. And as you know, we used to manage the forests to assure that we had vital, healthy forests. We removed excess timber before it could choke off the forest and burn. From that, we produced a steady stream of revenue and commerce for the region that supported our local communities, supported thriving economies throughout the Sierra. When we passed laws in the 1970s that made the management of our forests all but impossible, we've watched them do what an untended garden will do, and that is grow and grow until it chokes itself to death. And that's the condition of our forest today. That's why I've served on the Natural Resources Committee now for 11 years to try to restore the laws that allowed for the proper maintenance of our forests. And of course the economy, now we have that tremendous success there. The tax reductions and regulatory reforms that we've been able to win over the last couple of years are produced one of the most profound economic expansions in our nation's history. and we're seeing that across the country. Lowest unemployment rate in 50 years. Lowest unemployment rate for women since the 1950s. Lowest unemployment rate for Americans of African and Hispanic descent since they began keeping records. So we've had some significant successes there. We've had some successes in forest management. The legislation that I was able to get into the WIN Act is provided for expedited forest thinning in the Tahoe Basin, which has taken the bureaucratic delays from years down to months has shrunk the necessary environmental assessment from 800 pages down to less than 40, and is starting to show results there. We need to get those same reforms enacted for the entire national forest system, but I think we can now make a pretty good case on that.

turn_text: Well, exactly. And I was struck by something that Jerry Brown said after the campfire that wiped out the town of Paradise, killed 86 people. He said, well, this is the new abnormal. And I went back and did some looking at that and found out it's not the new abnormal at all. It's the old normal. In the last half of the 20th century, We lost about 250,000 acres a year in California to catastrophic fire. It was very steady, very consistent, about 250,000 acres. Last year, we lost one and a half million acres to catastrophic wildfire. something very bad has happened. But when we look at the destruction of paradise, we forget that was about 150,000 acres. In 1910, the big burn destroyed three million acres in Montana and Idaho, wiped out six towns and killed 87 people among a much sparser population than we have today. It was right around that time that we formed the US Forest Service. The Forest Service's job was to protect the forest, to manage them properly. And as I said, an untended forest is like an untended garden. If you leave it alone and don't tend to it, it's going to choke itself to death and ultimately will be consumed by catastrophic fire. And if you go back into the pre-Columbian days, you'll see that's exactly what happened. Prior to the discovery of California, the paleontologists tell us that in California, we would lose between 4.5 million and 12 million acres a year to catastrophic fire. That's what happens when the forests aren't properly managed. That's nature's way of dealing with it. Because of good management, we brought that from between four and a half and 12 million acres a year down to only a quarter million. When we abandoned those policies in the 1970s, we've watched the acreage being consumed by fire grow dramatically. We've seen an 80% decline in timber harvested off the federal lands over the past 30 years since those laws took effect 40 years now. And we've also watched a concomitant increase in acres destroyed by fire. There's an old maxim that excess timber comes out of a forest one way or another. It's either carried out or it burns out, but it will come out. When we carried it out, we had healthy forests. We also had a thriving local economy. And since we consigned our forests back to a policy of benign neglect, we've watched them consumed by fire.

turn_text: Well, first let's just get a brief background of our water situation. Fortunately, we live in one of the most water-rich regions of the country in northern California. But, you know, everybody seems to think that the Colorado River is the great river in the West. Colorado River is a junior sister of the Sacramento. The Sacramento is a much, much larger river. The difference is we store 70 million acre feet of water on the Colorado. We only store 10 million acre feet on the Sacramento and lose most of the rest of that to the Pacific Ocean every year. What I learned, chairing the water committee for four years, is that droughts are nature's fault. They happen. But water shortages are our fault. Water shortages are a result of deliberate choice that we made to stop building dams. turn_text: Well, everything you need to know about the federal budget with three numbers, 26, 29, and 46. 26% is the increase of inflation population over the last 10 years. 29% is the increase in revenue. So our revenues, even after the tax cuts, have more than kept pace with inflation and population. In fact, after the tax cuts, we're actually taking in record amounts of new revenue because of the economic expansion that those tax cuts made possible. So 26% increase in inflation and population combined, 29% increase in revenues. Here's what's killing us. That third number, 46% is the increase in federal spending in the same period. We are spending vastly more than the growth of our revenues. And the result is catastrophic deficits. Now accumulated debt of more than $23 trillion. But what's really dangerous about that is the interest costs that we have to pay. We're paying about 400, very rough terms, about $400 billion a year just in interest. That's money going out the door from your tax. And when we talk about $1 billion, by the way, in federal money, Art Laffer calls those MEGO numbers, MEGO, my eyes glaze over. I've always found it important to use some real world standard. Every billion dollars we throw around in Washington, think of that as eight dollars from your family's budget because if you divide the number of families into a billion dollars, it's eight dollars. So when we talk about a trillion dollars, we're talking about eight thousand dollars out of your family's budget. When we talk about running up a one trillion, almost one trillion dollar deficit next year, That's $8,000 being added to your family's credit card bill. And this isn't theoretical. This is just as real as if it appeared on your credit card bill. In fact, it's more real because you're required to pay back that $8,000 before you can pay back the first dollar of your own debt. And the IRS is always very insistent that you do. That comes out of your future taxes. So this is absolutely killing our country. And so when you talk about $400 billion a year, just an interest cost, put that in perspective, our entire defense establishment right now costs about $700 billion. And the growth of the interest payments on that debt is so steep that they estimate within the next few years. We're going to be paying more just to rent money we've already spent then we're able to spend for the entire defense of our country. That is simply not sustainable and history is shouting this warning at us that countries that bankrupt themselves simply aren't around very long because before you can provide for the common defense or promote the general welfare, you've got to be able to pay for it and that debt is now threatening our country's future ability to do so. It's got to be brought under control and it's got to be brought under control on the spending side because that's what's driving it. And when you hear people say, oh, we need higher taxes. Well, first of all, higher taxes don't necessarily mean higher revenues. We've already learned that. There's a point where you raise taxes, you actually do so much damage to the economy. You bring in less revenue. We just cut taxes. And because of the positive impact that had on the economy, it's bringing in more revenues. The problem is on the spending side and that's what Congress has refused to address.
